commentary: Aquinas reads this opening chapter as Aristotle's account of how the mind stands toward the highest truths, the ones metaphysics itself pursues. The inquiry is easy in one sense: everyone, by natural light, grasps certain basic and self-evident starting points, so that no one is wholly shut out from truth, the way no one can wholly miss a doorway open to all. Yet it is hard in another sense, because possessing the whole of truth, or hitting the precise part one is aiming at, exceeds what any single mind can manage on its own; only the community of thinkers across time approaches completeness, each contributing a portion. Aquinas locates the deeper source of this difficulty not in the truths themselves but in the disproportion between our intellect and them: our understanding is naturally fitted to material, sensible things, and only weakly and derivatively able to reach immaterial and separate realities, much as the eye of a bat is overwhelmed by daylight. He also takes the occasion to reject the view, associated with Averroes, that human beings can attain full, connatural knowledge of separate substances in this life. Because earlier thinkers, even when mistaken, sharpened the tools of inquiry and prepared the way for those who came after, gratitude is owed to all of them, not only to those we agree with. Aquinas then explains why metaphysics deserves the name "knowledge of truth" above the other sciences: theoretical knowledge has truth itself as its very end, while practical knowledge subordinates truth to action; and since whatever most fully causes a quality in other things possesses that quality most eminently, the first and most universal causes of things must also be supremely and unqualifiedly true, more true than anything caused by them.

Here Aquinas follows Aristotle's demonstration that causes cannot proceed to infinity, treating the argument as applying, in turn, to every kind of cause distinguished in his philosophy: efficient, material, final, and formal. For efficient and moving causes, he reasons that if a series had no first member, every member would be a mere intermediate; but an intermediate cause only transmits the causality of something prior to it, so that if nothing were first, nothing could really explain anything, and the whole series would collapse into unintelligibility. For material causes, Aquinas carefully distinguishes two ways one thing is said to come from another: as the man comes from the boy, where the later state is the fulfillment of a potency already underway in the earlier, and as one element is generated from the corruption of another, where the coming-to-be of one is strictly the passing-away of its predecessor. Neither pattern, he argues, tolerates an infinite regress, since each requires a determinate boundary or terminus to make sense of the process at all; there must be some primary matter or ultimate subject beneath the changes. Turning to final causality, Aquinas insists that if ends receded infinitely, the very notion of a good or a purpose would be destroyed, since something is called good precisely as a terminus that other things are for; and no agent, natural or intellectual, could act at all if it had no determinate end in view, since purposeful motion requires a limit toward which it tends. Finally, regarding formal causes and definitions, Aquinas explains that a definition cannot be endlessly resolved into further defining terms, because prior, more universal terms already contain and explain what is proper to what follows; an infinite regress here would make science and definition impossible, since nothing could ever be fully grasped or known if understanding always awaited one more term.

In this final chapter Aquinas takes up Aristotle's remarks on method, reading them as a caution about the proper way to receive philosophical teaching. He observes that a listener's habituation shapes what kind of exposition seems fitting to him, since long custom comes to function almost like a second nature, forming an expectation of how truth ought to be presented. This is why, he notes, even fabulous or childish elements retained in old laws can carry more persuasive weight with the untrained than sound reasoning does, simply because people are accustomed to them. Different audiences, accordingly, demand different modes of proof: some trust only mathematical demonstration, others need concrete examples, others look to cite poets or established authorities as witnesses, and still others insist on painstaking exactness in every point, while some are irritated by such exactness and regard it as needless fussiness, much as some regard scrupulous dealing in trade as somehow petty. Aquinas draws from this the methodological lesson that one must already be trained, through a prior grounding in logic, to recognize which kind of argument is proper to which kind of subject matter, since it is unreasonable to seek both the knowledge itself and the correct manner of pursuing it at the very same time. He then applies this principle directly to the limits of mathematical precision: such rigor is appropriate only where the subject matter is free of matter, that is, in immaterial or abstract objects, but cannot reasonably be demanded in natural philosophy, whose subject is bodies involving matter and therefore admits only conclusions that hold for the most part rather than with strict necessity.
